title: How Primark Makes Money Without Selling Online

beats.say: Primark barely advertises. For years it didn't sell a single thing online. And it still brings in more than nine billion pounds a year.

vis.text: No big ads. No online shop. £9.5 billion.

beats.say: In a world where every shop is fighting to sell on your phone, Primark did the opposite. It made you come to it. So how does that work?
In its financial year to September twenty twenty five, Primark's sales were about nine and a half billion pounds, and it made around one point one billion pounds in operating profit.

vis.title: Primark, financial year 2025
vis.source: Associated British Foods full year results, FY2025

beats.say: That's roughly twelve pence of profit from every pound you spend there. Not bad for a shop that sells t-shirts for a few quid.

vis.label: profit from every £1 spent (adjusted operating margin 11.9%)

beats.say: Part one. Where it came from.

Primark started in Dublin in nineteen sixty nine, under the name Penneys. It still trades as Penneys in Ireland today. It's owned by a big British company called Associated British Foods, which also makes Kingsmill bread and Twinings tea.

events: Expands into the UK as Primark

beats.say: From the start, the idea was simple. Fashionable clothes, at prices so low that people buy more than they planned.

vis.text: Prices so low you buy more than you planned.

beats.say: And Primark's shops are huge. Some of its biggest stores are like department stores, with several floors of clothes, homeware, beauty and even cafés. The bigger the shop, the longer people stay, and the more they buy.

vis.title: Why the shops are so big

beats.say: Location matters just as much. Primark chooses busy high streets and shopping centres, where crowds of people walk past every day anyway. The building itself is the advert.
Part two. Volume, not margin.
Primark makes only a little on each item. The trick is selling an enormous number of them. Huge orders from factories mean lower prices for each piece of clothing.
Primark also keeps its designs simple and copies trends quickly. When a style is popular, it can be in the shops fast, at a fraction of the price of the brand that started it.
Part three. No big adverts.

Most fashion brands spend a fortune on adverts. Primark has always spent very little on traditional advertising. Instead, it relies on its shops, word of mouth, and people showing off their bargains on social media.
The famous Primark haul video does the advertising for free. Someone fills three brown bags, films what they got for fifty pounds, and millions of people watch.
Every pound Primark doesn't spend on adverts is a pound it can use to keep prices low.

vis.text: No ad budget means lower prices.

beats.say: There's another trick hidden in the shop itself. Primark's shelves are packed and slightly messy, a bit like a market. It feels like a treasure hunt. You dig through a pile, find something for four pounds, and it feels like a win.
Part four. Why not sell online?

Here's the surprising part. Selling cheap clothes online is expensive. Every order has to be picked, packed, posted and often returned. On a three pound t-shirt, the delivery could cost more than the shirt.
In a shop, you do the work yourself. You walk in, pick it up, try it on and carry it home. Primark's costs stay low because the customer becomes the delivery driver.

vis.title: In the shop, you do the work

beats.say: And there's another bonus. In a shop, people spend more than they planned. You go in for socks, and you leave with a bag full of things you saw on the way to the tills.

vis.text: In for socks. Out with a bag full.

beats.say: Part five. Things are changing.

Primark has slowly moved online, but on its own terms. It started a click and collect trial in two thousand and twenty two. By May twenty twenty five, it was available in a hundred and eighty seven stores across England, Scotland and Wales.

events: Click and collect trial in 25 shops

beats.say: Click and collect is clever. You still have to come to the shop to pick up your order, and while you're there, you'll probably buy something else. Primark has also said home delivery will come in Britain in the future.

Primark has also kept growing in the United States and across Europe, opening new stores while many other clothing chains closed theirs. Its owner has even reviewed whether Primark should become a separate company in future, because it has grown so big.

vis.text: Primark keeps opening shops as rivals close
vis.date: Its owner is reviewing whether to separate it

beats.say: So what's the catch? Very cheap clothes raise big questions about the people who make them, and about how many clothes end up thrown away. Primark says it's working on both, but they're fair questions to ask about any cheap fashion.

vis.title: The fair questions
items: Who made it, and how were they paid?
What happens when it's thrown away?

beats.say: But as a business, the formula is clear. Sell a lot. Spend little on adverts. Let customers do the delivery. And make the shop so cheap that a quick look turns into a full bag.

vis.title: The Primark formula
items: Turn a look into a full bag

beats.say: So the next time you leave Primark with a bag you didn't plan to buy, you're not just a customer. You're the delivery driver, the advert and the profit.

vis.text: You're the driver, the advert and the profit.
